doc.title: Ray Bryant interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Learning 'After Hours' and playing it with Erskine Hawkins
summary: Bryant learned Avery Parrish's 'After Hours' from the Erskine Hawkins record, recorded it c.1958, and later sat in with Hawkins's band on a jazz cruise.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I would like to read a little quote that was written about you from the All Music Guide to Jazz. The fellow said: “Although he could always play bop, Ray Bryant combines older elements including blues, boogie woogie, Gospel, and stride into a distinctive soulful and swinging style. No one plays ‘After Hours’ quite like him.” Nice comment, huh?

Yeah it’s nice, especially since “After Hours” is one of my favorite tunes. I think it’s one of the first piano selections that I actually learned. I learned it from the original recording by Erskine Hawkins, featuring Avery Parrish at the piano. I mean it’s a composition of Mr. Parrish, and as I said it’s one of the first tunes that I learned. And I’ve been playing it all my life and I still enjoy playing it.
Can you tell me how you learned it? Did you learn it from listening to the recording, or did you get the sheet music to it, or was it a compilation?
No I learned it just from listening to the recording.
So you were listening to a large ensemble and bringing it down to the piano.

Well the piano was featured in the orchestra. It was a feature piano thing. Actually it was like a trio recording right up until the very end of the tune, then the band comes in on the last chorus and plays a little riff behind the piano, and so it was basically a piano recording within the band, the Erskine Hawkins Orchestra. I really, really love this tune, and I finally, all my life it was a dream of mine to play this song with Erskine Hawkins, because you know I made a recording of it with Dizzy Gillespie and Sonny Rollins back around 1958, and the recording got to be pretty popular. A lot of people even accused me

of playing it better than Avery Parrish, which I never believed, never, not for a minute. So anyway, I was on a boat cruise, on a jazz cruise once and Erskine Hawkins’ band was on the cruise also, and I met Mr. Hawkins and I just came out and asked him, I said, “Mr. Hawkins, I learned ‘After Hours’” — he knew who I was, he knew that I wasn’t just anybody, he knew that I could play — I said, “Could I come in and play this tune with the band one night?” He says, “Sure, come by tonight around ten o’clock and let me know you’re there, and we’re on.” I did it and I played it with the orchestra, I knew the whole arrangement and everything else. It was one of the dreams of my life, came true.
